opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic picture I have is that most of the progress we've seen in AI over the past decade or so has been driven by scaling up compute. If you look at frontier training runs, the amount of compute has been growing by something like four or five times per year. Algorithmic progress matters too, and it's substantial, but a lot of that progress is itself downstream of having more compute, because you need compute to run experiments and discover which ideas actually work at scale.

So if you ask what happens when that compute growth slows down, the answer is that progress slows down too, unless something else picks up the slack. And there are fairly concrete reasons to expect it to slow. Right now we're scaling by increasing spending enormously, not just by chips getting cheaper. Hardware price-performance improves maybe 30 to 40 percent per year, so most of the growth comes from people simply spending more money. You can do that for a while, going from millions to billions to tens of billions of dollars, but at some point you're talking about a meaningful fraction of world GDP, and that's not something you can keep multiplying by a few times every year.

There are also physical bottlenecks: power, data center construction, chip fabrication capacity, high-bandwidth memory, and so on. Those can be expanded, but they take years. You can't build a new fab or a few gigawatts of generation overnight.

So my view is that we probably have something like the rest of this decade where scaling can continue at roughly the current pace, and after that it likely has to slow toward the rate at which the underlying economy and hardware efficiency grow. If AGI, in the sense of systems that can actually do most of the work humans do, requires substantially more effective compute than we'll reach by then, and I think it plausibly does, given how much current systems still struggle with things like agency, long-horizon tasks, and the messy reality of real jobs, then the timeline gets stretched out quite a bit. You go from a world where every couple of years you get another order of magnitude to one where each order of magnitude takes much longer.

That's why I tend to be more skeptical of very short timelines. It's not that I think progress will stop. It's that the engine driving it has a limited runway at its current speed, and people often extrapolate recent trends without asking what's actually sustaining them.

r001.rationale: It says compute is needed to run experiments and find which ideas work at scale, suggesting software progress can be bottlenecked by available compute.

r002.rationale: It says scaling may slow unless something else picks up the slack, but does not suggest that early AGI could create economic feedback to sustain rapid compute scaling.

r003.rationale: It explains that scaling depends increasingly on enormous spending and cannot keep multiplying once it reaches a meaningful fraction of world GDP.

r004.rationale: It contrasts faster and slower compute scaling and their effects on timelines, but does not connect more orders of magnitude per year to a higher annual probability of reaching AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the basic picture I have is that most of the progress we've seen in AI over the past decade or so has been driven by scaling up compute. Algorithmic improvements matter too, but when you decompose where the capabilities came from, a very large fraction of it is just that we're training models with something like four or five times more compute every year, and that rate has been pretty consistent since around 2010.

The problem is that this growth rate is not sustainable indefinitely, and the reason is that it has been achieved mostly by increasing spending rather than by hardware getting cheaper. Hardware efficiency improves maybe at a rate of a doubling every two or three years, but compute spending on frontier training runs has been growing much faster than that. So the gap is being filled by companies putting more and more money into these runs. Right now we're talking about training runs that cost on the order of billions of dollars, and if you extrapolate the current trend, you get to tens or hundreds of billions within a few years, and then you hit a point where the cost of a single training run is a non-trivial fraction of global GDP. Obviously that can't continue.

So the question is when exactly you hit the wall. And my view is that we probably have a few more years, maybe until the end of this decade, where scaling can continue at roughly the current pace, because there's still a lot of willingness to invest, and there's a lot of room to build out power and chip manufacturing capacity. But after that, you'd need the growth to be justified by actual revenue from AI systems, and the question is whether AI will be economically valuable enough by then to pay for its own continued scaling.

If it is, then scaling continues, maybe at a somewhat slower pace. If it isn't, then you're in a situation where compute growth falls back to something like the hardware efficiency trend, maybe a doubling every couple of years, and that's a dramatic slowdown. At that point progress depends much more on algorithmic improvements, and those are harder to count on, because it's not clear how much low-hanging fruit is left there once you don't have the compute growth to complement it.

There's also a more fundamental point, which is that even hardware efficiency improvements are running into limits. Moore's law is slowing down, there are physical constraints on how much you can shrink transistors, and the energy costs of running these systems are becoming a serious bottleneck. So the long-run picture is one where compute growth is constrained by energy and manufacturing, and AGI, if it requires something like a few more orders of magnitude of effective compute beyond what we have now, might be delayed by that.

I should say that I don't think this means AGI is impossible or very far off. It just means that the simple extrapolation of "scale continues at the current pace until we get there" is probably not right. The more likely path involves a slowdown, and then progress is governed by the slower trends, which pushes timelines out compared to what you'd get from naively extending the current curve.

r001.rationale: The response says slower compute growth would make progress depend more on algorithmic improvements, but does not say compute availability constrains experimentation in AI software.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems might generate enough revenue to sustain scaling, but does not connect sufficiently early AGI to that economic feedback.

r003.rationale: It says current scaling is funded by rapidly growing spending, projects training runs reaching tens or hundreds of billions, and concludes that this growth cannot continue indefinitely.

r004.rationale: The response discusses compute growth and AGI timelines, but does not suggest that traversing more orders of magnitude of compute per year raises the annual probability of reaching AGI.

astra-6.text:
The basic reason is that a lot of recent progress has come from training models with more compute. If that becomes harder to sustain, then one of the main engines of progress slows down.

There are several potential constraints. You have to manufacture the chips, build the data centers, and supply the electricity. And someone has to pay for all of that. Even if a larger training run is technically feasible, it might not be economically attractive if the expected improvement doesn’t justify the cost.

But I’d distinguish slowing progress from putting a hard ceiling on it. We can still get better algorithms, use data more efficiently, and find better ways to use existing models. The question is how quickly those improvements can substitute for increases in compute.

So the implication for AGI depends on how far away it is. If the methods we have only need a modest amount of additional scaling, these constraints might not matter very much. If they need many more orders of magnitude of compute, then sustaining the recent pace becomes much more difficult. That’s why I think compute limits are a reason to be cautious about simply extrapolating recent progress forward.

r001.rationale: It says much recent progress came from training with more compute and that difficulty sustaining this slows a main engine of progress, linking available compute to AI progress.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that reaching AGI early would create economic feedback that sustains rapid compute scaling.

r003.rationale: It says a training run may not be economically attractive if its improvement does not justify its cost, but does not identify growing compute costs relative to available investment as a constraint on maintaining the current scaling rate.

r004.rationale: It mentions needing many more orders of magnitude of compute, but does not connect the amount scaled per year to the annual probability of reaching AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that a lot of recent progress has come from using more compute. You train larger models, you train them on more data, and you get better performance. But if you want to keep doing that, you need to keep increasing the resources devoted to training, and there are constraints on how quickly you can do that.

Some of those constraints are economic. Even if a training run is technically feasible, somebody has to pay for the chips and the electricity. Others involve how quickly you can manufacture chips, build data centers, and supply power to them. So a trend that looks very rapid while the industry is relatively small might become harder to sustain as it gets larger.

That doesn't mean progress stops, because compute isn't the only input. You can improve algorithms and use the compute you have more efficiently. The question is whether those improvements can compensate for slower growth in compute, and how much additional scaling we actually need to reach AGI. If we need substantially more than we have today, then constraints on scaling could make the timeline considerably longer.

r001.rationale: The response says compute enables better model performance, but does not identify compute availability as a bottleneck for AI software experimentation.

r002.rationale: It mentions economic constraints but does not suggest that early AGI could create feedback that sustains rapid compute scaling.

r003.rationale: It notes that chips and electricity must be paid for and that scaling may get harder, but does not say compute costs are growing relative to available investment.

r004.rationale: It does not connect traversing more orders of magnitude of compute scale per year with a higher annual probability of reaching AGI.
